data.title: Kimi’s AI credit card turns spending into computing quotas – with limits
data.description:
China’s artificial intelligence companies have spent years persuading consumers to pay for their technology. Now, Moonshot AI, the start-up behind Kimi, is taking a different approach: offering AI computing benefits through a credit card.
The company has teamed up with the Agricultural Bank of China (ABC) and American Express for what it calls “the world’s first AI native credit card”. After getting one for myself, the experience offered an intriguing way to bring AI services into everyday finance, but with limits to the promise.
The card comes in two versions. The premium platinum offers cardholders two months of Kimi’s second most expensive Allegretto membership, now rebranded as Pro, priced at 199 yuan (US$30) per month, after they spend at least 5,888 yuan (US$830) within one month.
The standard version offers eligible new ABC customers three months of the entry-level Andante membership, now known as Go, priced at 49 yuan per month, after making three purchases of at least 18 yuan each.
My initial attempt to obtain the higher-end card was denied at an ABC branch in Beijing, where I was told that my annual income did not meet the requirement. In my case, the requirements focused on traditional banking eligibility rather than anything related to AI use.
I then applied online for the standard card, and eventually received it within a week.

The Kimi co-branded card, launched in July, followed a wave of AI-themed bank cards introduced by Chinese lenders since June. China Merchants Bank’s engineer card, for example, mainly gives new users a one-off token gift pack. But the Kimi card promises to turn everyday spending into access to AI services, including agent usage quotas, coding tools and premium subscriptions.
The Andante membership that came with my card provides additional access to Kimi’s AI agent functions, including document processing, website deployment and coding capabilities.
For a frequent AI user, the rewards are more attractive than shopping vouchers or airport lounge access provided by traditional credit cards.
With the benefits, I tried vibe coding, asking Kimi to refine the visual design and interactive features of a project.
The experience was initially promising. But after roughly six rounds of adjustments, Kimi informed me that my usage quota had been exhausted.
It was a frustrating reminder that access to premium AI services does not necessarily mean having unlimited usage quotas to complete a task.
There are also limits to how long you have access. For example, the memberships that came with the card were just for a few months, not permanent subscriptions.
Neither Moonshot, ABC nor Amex responded to requests for comment.
Moonshot and its partners previously said they would explore additional services, such as agent-based payments, linking tokens to credit quotas, and establishing two-way integration between reward points and computing power.
The push into AI-focused financial services comes as China’s credit card market contracts. The country had 677 million credit cards and debit-credit combo cards at the end of June, down from 807 million in the third quarter of 2022, according to the People’s Bank of China.
Wang Zebin, an investment manager at Shenzhen-based private equity firm JG Investment who focuses on AI investments, said the shift towards computing-based rewards reflected banks’ efforts to attract and retain high-net-worth customers through more targeted offerings.
Whether such products can generate meaningful long-term growth for banks’ credit card business would depend on how lenders integrated AI into their operations, improved credit approvals and risk management, and sustained investment in the AI computing ecosystem, Wang said.

data.title: Man arrested for alleged HK$450,000 theft of wife’s Chanel, Hermes, Rolex goods
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested the husband of a 34-year-old woman for allegedly stealing luxury goods worth HK$450,000 (US$57,700) from her at home.
The woman, surnamed Chan, reported the case to police at around 8.30am on Saturday morning at their home in the Ocean One residential development in Yau Tong.
According to police, Chan suspected that her 40-year-old husband, surnamed Lam, had stolen goods worth HK$450,000 in total. The items involved were Chanel and Hermes bags worth HK$300,000 and a HK$150,000 Rolex watch.
Police later arrived at the scene and arrested Lam on suspicion of theft after a preliminary investigation. He is currently being detained for further investigation.

data.title: Beijing enlists multiple regulators to probe EV safety issue
data.description:
Beijing has enlisted the support of its top internet watchdog to deepen the investigation into a car safety issue that put Chinese-made intelligent vehicles under the spotlight.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) said on Thursday that a joint investigation team including officials from the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) and the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) would verify facts regarding reports about brake pedal failures in tests of an electric vehicle (EV) made by the Huawei Technologies-backed Maextro luxury brand.
The three ministry-level authorities “have paid close attention to the issue”, the MIIT said. “Relevant information will be released in a timely manner.”
The statement showed that Chinese authorities would be resolute in addressing concerns about Chinese EV quality and reliability amid a falling domestic market, analysts said.
On October 8, ByteDance-owned car-information platform Dongchedi released a video showing that brake-pedal brackets snapped on all three Maextro V800 multipurpose vehicles used in a test of emergency braking from 100km/h.
The video went viral, while Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said in a commentary on Sunday that the incident underscored the importance of strengthened oversight over the country’s “rapidly developed” EVs.
“The internet regulator will be responsible for sifting out misinformation [about the matter] online that could taint the reputation of Chinese carmakers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “Consumers will be eager to see the truth amid regulators’ heightened investigation efforts.”
Maextro, jointly developed by Huawei and JAC and based in eastern China’s Anhui province, said in a statement on Thursday that it would fully cooperate with the investigation team to safeguard the interests of consumers and support the development of China’s EV industry.


On Sunday, the brand said that it would address the brake pedal issue by the end of this month. JAC assembles Maextro vehicles. Tech giant Huawei, through its Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance, supplies technology for smart driving and digital cockpits to the EVs.
The Maextro V800 is one of the most expensive EV models in mainland China, with a base price of 766,000 yuan (US$113,582).
On Saturday, the MIIT, along with three other ministry-level departments, published draft rules stipulating that sufficient vetting measures including 30,000km (18,641 miles) of road testing should be completed before any new model was offered to consumers.
Car sales in China slumped 21.7 per cent year on year to 13.3 million units in the first nine months of 2026 due to narrowing government support such as smaller EV purchase subsidies and a resumption of consumption tax.
In August, MIIT vice-minister Xin Guobin said at a press briefing in Beijing that new auto products and technologies would be barred from entering the market unless they passed stricter approval procedures.
Beijing is also carrying out a nationwide inspection campaign assessing the quality of Chinese-made cars.

data.title: Shisha smoking will cause 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050: WHO
data.description:
Water pipe smoking will contribute to about 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050, with the Western Pacific region bearing the brunt, according to a study led by a World Health Organization (WHO) research agency that was recently presented in Hong Kong.
The study, which is yet to be published, was headed by Dr Mahdi Sheikh, a scientist of the early detection, prevention and infections branch at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). It estimated that there would be 82 million new lung cancer cases around the world between 2025 and 2050, with 944,700 or 1.1 per cent of them caused by water pipe smoking.
“One per cent does not seem a lot, but when you translate it into numbers, it’s 1 million cases – when we want to save lives, every life matters,” Sheikh told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress, which was held in Hong Kong for the first time in late September.
“Most of these countries have a low or medium human development index … it means that the burden is going to cluster in the countries with the least resources, which could bear the least burden of cancer.”
Traditional cigarettes remained the primary cause of lung cancer, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of cases, alongside other risk factors such as air pollution and occupational exposure, he said.

Combining data on water pipe prevalence, cancer risk and WHO projections across 78 countries, the research team estimated that the Western Pacific region would see 350,400 new cases of water pipe-related lung cancer over the 25-year period.
This was followed by 265,700 cases in the European region.
In terms of proportion of cases relative to population, the Eastern Mediterranean region, largely covering countries such as the Middle East, topped the chart with 5.1 per cent, followed by the African region with 2.6 per cent.
Notably, countries which were among the least developed, as indicated by their low Human Development Index, would suffer the heaviest proportional toll, with water pipes causing 3.3 per cent of their lung cancer cases, followed by countries of the medium index at 1.8 per cent.
Sheikh said the Western Pacific region topped the total case count because it contained countries with either high exposure to water pipe smoking or massive populations.
The Eastern Mediterranean region, meanwhile, held the highest water pipe smoking rates globally due to deep historical roots and rising popularity among younger generations.
“The tobacco industry is coming up with strategies to increase the use of these products among the youth [there],” Sheikh said.
“If young people use these products today, the impact will be obvious two decades from now. We need to raise awareness before this happens.”
Sheikh noted that manufacturers added flavours and framed water pipe use as a social activity to entice youth while spreading disinformation that water filtered out toxic substances.
However, unlike traditional cigarettes, water pipe smoking received far less regulatory scrutiny despite the WHO issuing its first guidelines more than two decades ago, he added.
According to the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, 79 per cent of parties to the treaty reported water pipe tobacco on their national markets in 2023, but only 57 per cent had implemented specific regulations.
“The guideline is there. Some countries have worked; a lot of countries still lag behind and are way behind [on regulations for] combustible tobacco products,” Sheikh said.
A major shortcoming was the lack of monitoring, as the research team could only obtain data from 78 countries, with severe data gaps in Africa and the Western Pacific.
“The burden is much, much bigger than what we think … I believe there is a lot of underestimation,” he said.
“One of the basic policies that we require at WHO is monitoring.”

While further studies are under way, Sheikh urged countries to implement the guidelines of the global health watchdog and guard against tobacco industry interference.
In this process, he believed Hong Kong could serve as a successful example, pointing to its single-digit smoking prevalence rate.
Hong Kong’s smoking rate is 8.5 per cent, while the rate of water pipe smoking is less than 1 per cent.
“The guidelines are there, the policies are there, and we see some countries are extremely successful with that,” he said.
“We have to work together to prevent the interference [of the tobacco industry]. They should not have a seat at the table. They are the ones that cause this problem, and they should be accountable for that.”

data.title: Police receive over 100 reports about credit card charges for iPhone Duo pre-orders
data.description:
Hong Kong police have received more than 100 reports of unauthorised credit card transactions related to pre-orders of Apple’s latest iPhone model, the South China Morning Post has learned.
Apple began its online pre-orders for its foldable iPhone Duo on Friday at 8pm, and complaints about suspicious transactions began to appear on social media overnight.
Some credit card users claimed duplicate or unauthorised purchases of the new model.
A source said the transactions involved a few million Hong Kong dollars, but the amount was still rising.
It is the second time iPhones have been involved in unauthorised credit card transactions in just over a month, with the previous round concerning pre-orders of the iPhone 18 Pro series on September 12.
In response to media inquiries on Saturday, Apple said all current iPhone Duo orders were being reviewed before they were processed.
“[We] are working to quickly identify and cancel any fraudulent transactions that may have been placed,” the company said.

HSBC said it was aware of online discussions about repeated and unauthorised credit card transactions for the pre-orders.
“Customers will not be responsible for repeated transactions, which we will identify and void,” the bank said.
HSBC added that customers who identified unauthorised transactions could suspend their credit cards via its mobile app or by calling the bank.
The bank said it would investigate and guide consumers through the refund process, while noting they had a responsibility to use their cards responsibly and report suspicious transactions promptly.
It also said 3D Secure could add protection, but the merchant determined whether it applied.
3D Secure helps authenticate the buyer’s identity during online transactions.
HSBC reportedly apologised to affected consumers, noting that some transactions were duplicated on Friday night and the system would automatically arrange cancellation, which was expected to take one to two days.
Victims took to social media platform Threads on Friday night, with one user claiming to have ordered an iPhone Duo after 8pm using an HSBC credit card and being charged again at around 10pm.
Another user who reported a similar problem called the card centre, which said Apple sought HSBC’s authorisation a second time to complete the transaction and the first one was pending cancellation.
A separate user who said they had not ordered the new iPhone posted two SMS records from HSBC, which indicated their credit card had been charged twice by Apple.
In late September, police said they had received 1,503 reports over suspicious credit card transactions involving the iPhone 18 Pro series, totalling more than HK$30 million (US$3.82 million).
Preliminary investigations indicated that the online pre-order transactions did not require a one-time password via SMS or any other form of authentication, causing the payment process to be completed without the cardholder’s confirmation and allowing fraudsters to exploit the vulnerability.
Apple said last month that it was reviewing all its current orders to identify and cancel suspicious transactions. Major Hong Kong banks said victims would not be held liable, provided the transactions were proven unauthorised and cardholders had acted with due care.
The price of the Duo begins at HK$17,499, and the model will be available from October 23.

data.title: Alibaba to embed AI throughout Taobao, Tmall merchant operations in 2027
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding’s two major domestic online marketplaces, Taobao and Tmall, plan to greatly expand the use of artificial intelligence across merchants’ operations next year, a senior executive said, as the e-commerce giant doubles down on the technology to drive growth amid a challenging consumer landscape.
“Starting next year, AI will comprehensively enter the internal enterprise workflows of merchants,” Liu Bo, president of Tmall, said at the company’s Singles’ Day media briefing on Thursday.
An important product driving the push would be Qwen Work, Alibaba’s enterprise AI assistant, Liu added. The e-commerce version of the assistant began testing earlier this week and is designed for merchants selling across multiple platforms.
The move comes after the roll-out of AI on Taobao and Tmall over the past year “exceeded expectations”, Liu said, adding that merchants were already using platform-level AI tools for product launches, advertising and customer service.
The remarks came ahead of Alibaba’s annual Singles’ Day shopping festival, with official sales set to begin next Tuesday and a record 1 million global brands expected to take part. The company, which launched the event in 2009, is using this year’s festival as a testing ground for AI-driven growth.
Alibaba has aggressively rolled out AI-powered tools to consumers and merchants as it grapples with intense competition from rivals including JD.com and PDD Holdings.
The company said this year’s festival would feature deeper integration of its flagship Qwen AI model across its e-commerce ecosystem. For consumers, a Qwen-powered shopping assistant launched in May is designed to help users compare products, virtually try on clothes and select promotional discounts.
According to Liu, young, active Taobao and Tmall users currently buy goods from an average of 15 product categories annually. He said the platforms aimed to expand that figure to between 25 and 30 categories by using AI to better connect shoppers with a wider range of products.
“AI allows us to open up a larger vision,” Liu said. “It can match the rich supply of goods with the diverse demands of the crowd in ways traditional algorithms simply could not achieve.”
Alibaba is also introducing “AI tokens” as a new product category on its platforms. The company is partnering with major Chinese AI model developers, including Z.ai and MiniMax, to sell computing power directly to end users.
The tokens would be packaged into customised bundles tailored for different groups of users such as students, researchers and small teams, Liu said.
Tmall is also partnering with hardware giants such as Intel and Advanced Micro Devices to sell personal computers with Qwen models pre-installed.
Alibaba’s first large-scale deployment of generative AI across Taobao and Tmall came during the same event in 2025, when it integrated large language models into its core search and recommendation engines.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

data.title: Abby Choi’s partner tells murder trial she hid ex-in-laws’ dependence on her
data.description:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner has told a court she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute.
Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man.
During the third week of Choi’s murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background.
After an acrimonious row over parenting in mid-2022, Choi told Tam for the first time that she had been supporting the Kwong family financially and urged him and his father to cut ties with them.
But Tam said he and Choi had kept up a friendly facade in front of her former in-laws while seeking to sell a HK$72 million home registered in Kwong’s father’s name.
He acknowledged he had been “a bit sneaky”, but said this was unavoidable as the couple tried to recover what belonged to them gradually and through diplomatic means.
Asked whether he still viewed his former classmate in the same way after the dispute, Tam said: “I would say the friendship was no more.”
Kwong, 31, is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35.
The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial began last month.
Prosecutors argued that the murder stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of a luxury flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin.
They said Choi had registered her former father-in-law as the owner to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty but had never intended to give the property to her former in-laws.
The court heard that Choi had a heated argument with her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, at the Kadooria flat in June or July 2022, when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever.
Li allegedly told her son Alex to stay away from the child because she could infect him, prompting Choi to accuse her of favouring sons over daughters.
Kwong Kau allegedly joined the row, twice attempted to attack Choi, swore at her and called her a “birthing machine”.

The elder Kwong was subsequently barred from visiting the flat and seeing his two grandchildren. But the children were allegedly taken to see him and his girlfriend while Choi was attending a fashion event in France during the Chinese New Year holiday in 2023, much to her dismay.
Tam became friends with Alex Kwong in 2008, when they were studying at Concordia International School in Kowloon Tong, the court heard. Tam later continued his studies in Australia, while Kwong moved to Sear Rogers International School, where he met Choi.
Tam appeared surprised when Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, suggested he had wanted a “romantic and sexual relationship” with his client when they were schoolmates.
“Definitely disagree,” the witness said.
Tam said he first met Choi in late 2013 or early 2014, during a brief holiday visit to Hong Kong to see Kwong, who was then married to her.
He said his relationship with Choi changed after Kwong “totally disappeared” one day in 2015. That year, Kwong began divorce proceedings and absconded from a trial over his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case.
Tam and Choi began dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage, the court heard. Their daughter was born in September 2016 and their son three years later.
“After Abby and I were together, I knew through Abby that Kwong Kong-chi was fine with our relationship and sent us his blessing. I also know his relationship with Abby was something in the past,” Tam said.
He added that he and Choi would meet Kwong during leisure trips to mainland China. The three saw one another more often at family gatherings after Kwong returned to Hong Kong in 2022.
Asked whether they had remained close until Choi’s disappearance, Tam said it was reasonable for them to do so because of their children.
He said the Kwong brothers and their mother appeared calm and unconcerned after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023.
Li allegedly suggested that her former daughter-in-law had been abducted and that they should delay reporting her disappearance to police until the supposed kidnappers made their demands.
Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s stand-in driver at the time, allegedly evaded questions about her whereabouts and pretended to help by driving Tam around to look for her.
Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains were found at a rental flat in Lung Mei village, Tai Po, on February 24.
The trial also shed light on the Tam family’s wealth and financial dealings with Choi and her former in-laws.
Tam’s father, Tam Chak-kwan, founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian and received a share of the proceeds from its HK$1 billion sale to a Japanese company.

In 2019, the family moved into their current 4,000 sq ft home on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong, which the elder Tam bought for HK$168 million.
He said he had given his previous home, a 1,800 sq ft flat valued at HK$41 million at the Manhattan Hill private estate in Lai Chi Kok, to Choi in 2018. But he had not expected his de facto daughter-in-law to live there, as he wanted to share a home with his grandchildren.
The court heard that the elder Tam gave Choi at least HK$200,000 a month to cover living expenses for her and his son. He also gave her more than HK$80 million in total to invest.
Chris Tam said Choi had made money investing in luxury watches, although he was unsure whether she had done so through her ex-husband.
Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, accused Alex Kwong of failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million her daughter had given him to invest. She also called him a “brute” and dismissed his claim that he had supported her financially as “a pack of lies”.
Choi also put money into the Kadooria flat and an egg waffle shop run by Anthony Kwong, but Chris Tam said both had proved poor investments.
The court also heard how Kwong Kau had helped settle a dispute over a HK$5 million gambling debt Chris Tam incurred in Macau in August 2021.
The younger Tam said he had refused to repay the loan because he knew the casino, run by SunCity Group, was about to close following the arrest of its founder and CEO, Alvin Chau Cheok-wa.
Tam’s father said he had approached Kwong Kau for help because he wanted to resolve the dispute.
He said he had transferred HK$5 million to Kwong’s personal bank account in March 2022 and paid him a further HK$450,000 in gratuities for people with triad affiliations who had stopped debt collectors from harassing his family.
The elder Tam said Kwong Kau later asked him for a HK$400,000 loan, saying police had frozen his account. Tam agreed to lend him HK$250,000, which had yet to be repaid.
He added that he had ignored Kwong’s request for help with legal fees after the former officer was remanded in custody in connection with the case.
The trial continues on Tuesday before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

data.title: HSBC to double Hong Kong AI team to 300, outpacing Singapore planBank unveils expansion plan after scrutiny of its Singapore AI hiring strategy.
data.description:
HSBC, Hong Kong’s biggest lender, said on Thursday it would double its artificial intelligence specialist team in the city to 300, a figure much larger than the workforce planned for its recently announced AI centre in Singapore.
The announcement comes after Hong Kong’s regulators were reported to have raised concerns about the Singapore hub.
The bank would double its AI specialist headcount in Hong Kong from 150 to 300 over the next two to three years, said David Liao Yi-chien, HSBC co-CEO for Asia and the Middle East, in a media briefing after attending an industry event hosted by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).
HSBC would also launch the Hong Kong AI Institute next year, he said.
“Hong Kong is our home market at HSBC. We are using Hong Kong as the hub to develop our digital finance and embrace new technologies to better serve customers and support Hong Kong’s digital ambitions and growth,” Liao said.
Four members of the bank’s 13-member group operating committee were based in Hong Kong, underscoring the city’s importance to HSBC, he added.
The remarks marked the lender’s first public comments since it announced plans in late July to set up a Singapore AI centre and hire 100 specialists.
A source told the South China Morning Post last week that the HKMA had privately questioned HSBC about the decision.
Liao did not confirm the conversation with the HKMA, but said: “HSBC always has positive dialogues with the regulator.”
He said HSBC, as an international bank, “will always invest in AI in different markets, including mainland China, the UK and the Middle East, but Hong Kong will always be the core part of that investment”.
Hong Kong’s five-year plan, with AI as a pillar of development, “will give us a lot of opportunities”, Liao said. “HSBC has spent over [US$14 billion] on a buyout of shares from subsidiary Hang Seng Bank in January, which represents an important investment in Hong Kong.”
Liao spoke on the same day that the HKMA hosted an AI summit and highlighted use cases for the technology in Hong Kong’s finance sector.
Hong Kong’s development plan, with AI investment and development identified as a priority, could intensify competition with Singapore, analysts said.

The HKMA said on Thursday that 20 banks and 14 technology companies had completed sandbox testing of 27 AI use cases. HSBC alone contributed two use cases, including a language-to-sign-language translator for customers with hearing difficulties, and the use of AI to detect deepfakes during account opening.
The de facto central bank also announced new principles for banks’ use of AI, built around what it called the ART framework, which stood for accountability, resilience and trust. Under the principles, which took effect on Thursday, banks must appoint a responsible person for each AI application and maintain records of AI use cases and the associated risk-management measures.
In the coming weeks, the HKMA would also introduce a discussion paper on the governance of agentic AI and launch a platform for sharing AI training data, it said.
HKMA deputy CEO Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang said the discussion paper would focus on ensuring agentic AI systems operated according to their intended purpose and did not become “rogue agents”.
Banks would need a “kill switch” to stop agentic AI systems if they malfunctioned, while also maintaining fallback arrangements that allow human intervention to take over tasks when necessary, Yuen said, adding that the approach was aligned with international practices.
“The progression from generative to agentic AI represents an important new stage of innovation for the banking sector,” Yuen said.
Under Fintech 2030, the HKMA has encouraged banks to embrace AI, although such development must be supported by effective risk management and governance, he added.
“By pairing innovation with clear accountability, resilient operating models and effective human oversight, banks can fully realise the benefits of AI while maintaining the trust and stability of Hong Kong’s financial system,” Yuen said.

data.title: Hong Kong’s new Huanggang Port seemingly quiet ahead of expected holiday rush
data.description:
Hong Kong’s newly revamped Huanggang Port is expected to handle more than 100,000 passenger trips a day over the three-day Chung Yeung Festival holiday, but its departure hall remained quiet on Saturday morning.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said the port had operated smoothly since opening on Monday, handling about 80,000 passenger trips a day, with the figure exceeding 92,000 on Friday.
That represented a 1.5-fold to almost twofold increase from the 30,000 to 40,000 trips recorded before reconstruction, he said. Meanwhile, passenger trips at the Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau control points fell by between 3 and 7 per cent.
“As we already saw over 90,000 trips on Friday, I believe we would inevitably have over 100,000 trips during the peak [of Chung Yeung Festival holiday],” he said.
“We have the capacity to handle it, as the maximum capacity of the new port is at least 200,000 [trips].”
Tang said the authorities would deploy additional staff to allow all automated and manual clearance channels to open whenever needed. Staffing would also be increased at public transport pickup and drop-off points to prevent congestion.
He said waiting times were generally less than five minutes and no more than 15 minutes, with passengers often able to pass through the control point with almost no wait.
“While the duration is roughly the same as before, we need to consider that the passenger volume has more than doubled … and you just need to undergo one inspection to enter the mainland, without queuing again for a second check,” he said.
“If you look at it this way, the overall efficiency has effectively increased by at least fourfold, meaning it is four times as fast.”
Tang added that 300,000 residents had registered for “joint clearance” through a dedicated mobile app. The arrangement allows passengers to complete both departure and entry procedures by presenting the identity document required at their destination and passing through a three-gate automated channel.
A South China Morning Post reporter at Huanggang Port on Saturday morning saw travellers arriving by bus from across Hong Kong move swiftly into the departure hall, with almost no queues at the automated border control gates.

Hong Kong resident Yan Li, who usually visits Shenzhen about twice a month, said she had chosen Huanggang Port because the bus journey from Tai Wo Hau, with a change at Tai Lam Tunnel, was faster and cheaper than travelling via Lo Wu.
“My trip today cost HK$12.5 (2 US cents) and took me 45 minutes, compared with me using the Lo Wu port, which would be HK$48 and would take up to 80 minutes,” the trading professional in her thirties said, adding that the journey had been smooth overall.
Medical professional Michael Leung, a Hong Kong resident in his thirties, said he visited the mainland about once a month with his girlfriend or friends, usually staying in Shenzhen for food and massages.
“When borders first opened after the pandemic, we were drawn by good value for money on the mainland compared to Hong Kong, but that is not as pronounced any more because of the strengthened exchange rate,” he said, adding that he typically spent about HK$1,000 on a day trip to Shenzhen and usually tried restaurants or massage parlours he had not visited before.
“We go because it feels like a small getaway now.”
Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said on Saturday that rising fuel prices had posed a challenge to Hong Kong’s tourism sector this year by affecting short-haul visitor numbers.
She added that arrivals from Southeast Asia had declined.
“But visitor numbers from the mainland and long-haul markets remain favourable as they are attracted by many mega-events in Hong Kong,” she said.
“Since we have many upcoming mega-events, which will bring in a large number of visitors towards the end of the year, I am confident that the total number of visitors for the full year will reach 53.8 million as expected.”
Law said the opening of the new Huanggang Port on Monday was a positive development, giving tourists another crossing option and greater convenience.
“As the new Huanggang Port operates 24 hours a day, visitors would no longer feel rushed to return to the mainland; they can stay longer to eat or dine after concerts,” she said.

data.title: The butterfly effect: one man’s mission to help nature and communities coexist
data.description:
Hong Kong’s next phase of development should make room for both butterflies and buildings, conservationist Dr Yau Wing-kwong has said, arguing that biodiversity can be incorporated into parks, schools and neighbourhoods without holding back the city’s growth.
Yau, founder of Environmental Association Limited, has spent nearly three decades promoting community-based conservation. He is a finalist for the Spirit of Community Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.
His best-known project, the Fung Yuen Butterfly Reserve in Tai Po, began as an effort to protect butterfly habitats from collectors and other disturbances. It soon became an early example of a different approach to managing ecologically valuable private land.
Hong Kong announced its New Nature Conservation Policy in 2004, and Fung Yuen was among the first sites selected for a pilot management agreement scheme the following year. The arrangement allowed a non-profit organisation to work with private landowners, with government funding, to manage land for conservation.
“We did it almost like volunteers, with many volunteers and friends helping. We really made a model,” Yau said.
The pilot scheme later became part of Hong Kong’s conservation system, with similar management agreements introduced at other ecologically important sites.
Fung Yuen has long relied on community participation, with volunteers working alongside a small team of staff to maintain the reserve and support its conservation and education work.

Yau said volunteers help with planting, weeding and path maintenance, while university students join as interns. Retired teachers, civil servants and others also take on various roles.
“Volunteers sometimes receive an unexpected reward. When they are working, a butterfly may fly past or land on their shoulder,” he said. “They feel as if the butterfly has come to thank them.”
The reserve also conducts monthly surveys to monitor its ecology.
Yau said about 90 per cent of Hong Kong’s butterfly species had been recorded at Fung Yuen. He added that the discovery, within a single year, of seven species not previously recorded in the city, some associated with warmer areas further south.
Such sightings could offer clues about climate change, he said, although longer-term data were needed before firm conclusions could be drawn.
Conservation can also begin with everyday household habits. For more than a decade, the association has collected potted citrus trees discarded after Lunar New Year, as their leaves provide food for butterflies. Surplus trees are given to farmers, keeping them out of landfill and giving them a second life.
Yau believes the same approach can be applied as Hong Kong develops. Citing the Northern Metropolis, he said new parks and open spaces should provide wildlife habitats rather than focus mainly on ornamental greenery.
He said different planting choices could allow butterflies and other species to live in newly developed districts.

Hong Kong’s Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2035, updated in 2025, similarly calls for biodiversity conservation and sustainable development to advance together, with “harmony between humans and nature” among its stated goals.
Yau now wants to connect habitats beyond Fung Yuen. His interest in butterfly migration routes grew after a butterfly marked in Japan was found in Hong Kong following a journey of about 2,500km.
His concept is “point, line and surface”, in which individual butterfly gardens serve as points, flight routes connect them into lines, and enough connections eventually form a citywide network.
Schools across Hong Kong have joined Fung Yuen’s Butterfly Garden Certification Programme, and certified gardens have also been established in Shenzhen and Macau. The initiative has involved cooperation with organisations in Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Malaysia.
After nearly three decades, Yau said the work had also changed his understanding of conservation. Visitors could find calm in nature, while some students with special educational needs had become more communicative after helping to care for butterfly gardens.
“Protecting butterflies is also, in a way, protecting ourselves,” he said.
The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.
Yau has joined the race for Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll in November, standing in the Heung Yee Kuk subsector.
The elected members will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies, and select Hong Kong’s next chief executive in March next year.

data.title: Exclusive|Hong Kong touts features to set it apart from London in global gold hub push
data.description:
Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post.
In an exclusive interview on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city would officially launch a central gold clearing platform in the first quarter of next year. It would handle both physical delivery and payments, with the latter linked to the real-time gross settlement system.
Hui said the ultimate aim was to connect Asian liquidity with international market standards, giving participants a venue in the Asian time zone for trading, storage, clearing, refining and risk management.
“We are confident achieving [this] because in the Asia time zone we see Hong Kong as uniquely positioned to do that,” he said.
In the wide-ranging interview, Hui also discussed the city’s efforts to promote the international use of the yuan, the development of China’s digital currency, the e-CNY, and next week’s Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong.
Asked whether the Saudi Central Bank’s recent departure from mBridge had dealt a blow to the project, Hui said it would press ahead. The China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform is seen as an alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system.
The Saudi Central Bank, a key participant, confirmed last month that it had left the project after completing what it described as a limited proof-of-concept trial in May last year.
“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.
“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”
Hong Kong is a founding member and co-developer of mBridge.
The city is also accelerating the development of its gold trading ecosystem as a key part of its first five-year plan, which runs to 2030. The initiative is intended to support the development of mainland China’s gold economy, which combines the world’s largest domestic gold production and consumption markets.

Hui said government ownership and backing, integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement and cooperation with Shanghai would distinguish Hong Kong’s offering. The cross-border cooperation would allow eligible gold stored in the city to be used to settle trades in both markets.
Asked about competition with Singapore as a regional gold trading hub, Hui said Hong Kong was focused on improving its own performance.
“What Hong Kong tries to do is always to compete against ourselves because fundamentally we have to focus on areas that are within our control,” he said.
He expressed confidence in Hong Kong’s competitive advantages.
“What sets a global commodities market from the other markets is that it is really a market that is not just about financials but also close to the real economy,” he said.
“It has to be about also storage, about logistics, and also, at the same time, about trading, of course. And also when it comes to disputes, there could also be some legal issues.
“So actually, it’s a whole value chain in terms of the potential composition of this industry association to be set up before the end of this year.”
Hui added that following a trial in July, the integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement service was due to launch officially in the first quarter of next year.
“The clearing system now in the UK is run by the London Bullion Market Association, which is an industry association,” he said. “But the clearing house in Hong Kong is owned and run by the government. So I think this government backing sets us apart in terms of credibility.
“Another thing that is different between Hong Kong and London in that context is the fact that our current system will not just do physical delivery but also money settlement.”
Hui said 11 banks were already taking part in the payment settlement arrangements and others had expressed strong interest in joining, adding that the city would discuss cooperation on delivery standards with the London association.
Hui, who chairs the board overseeing the clearing facility, said a representative of the Shanghai Bourse served as deputy chair. Under the cross-border delivery connect arrangement, physical gold stored in certified Hong Kong vaults can be used to settle contracts traded in the local market and on Shanghai’s international board.

“If there is gold that is going to satisfy both the settlement in the Hong Kong contract and the Shanghai contract, they can use the vaults in Hong Kong, catering for both the Hong Kong market and the Shanghai market to do that,” he said. “It is an area that is uniquely Hong Kong.”
He added that the government was aiming to increase Hong Kong’s gold storage capacity to more than 2,000 tonnes within three years, with half at the airport and the remainder expected to come from the private sector.
Some gold refineries have also been established in the city.
Asked how Hong Kong could help the mainland gain greater influence over gold pricing, Hui said this would come once the city had attracted enough market participants and built sufficient liquidity.
“I see pricing more as an outcome, in the sense that once we build up a sufficient liquidity, at the same time a quantum of gold here, so it will eventually come,” he said, stressing the importance of building a critical mass of market participants.
On products, Hui highlighted the relaunch of a US dollar-denominated gold futures contract and said details of a yuan-denominated contract would be announced before the end of this year.
With this work under way, Hui hoped to share the latest developments in Hong Kong’s gold trading ecosystem when the city hosted the London Bullion Market Association Global Precious Metals Conference in April next year.
Reflecting on this month’s conference in Sorrento, Italy, which he attended, he said industry stakeholders had responded positively to Hong Kong’s plans.
“First of all, they are quite impressed in terms of the timeliness of this project, in a sense that in this world of changing geopolitics,” he said, adding that they were also impressed with the city’s ecosystem approach, its “concrete plans” and “Hong Kong speed”.
Hui said the initiative had progressed rapidly since its announcement in the October 2024 policy address.

data.title: A companion between appointments: Hong Kong student’s AI tool for cancer patients
data.description:
For cancer patients in Hong Kong, emotional distress can persist beyond the clinic, with a large combined analysis of multiple studies linking depression and anxiety to lower chances of survival.
Claudia Chan Shu-ying, a medical student at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), is developing CancerCompanion, a digital companion designed to offer emotional support between appointments, including late at night when professional help may not be immediately available.
The system uses AI-powered conversations to offer structured support while directing medical questions to healthcare teams and flagging potential cases of self-harm for human review.
Chan is a finalist in the youth category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. She is taking a year out from her medical degree to complete a master’s degree in research medicine.
The project grew out of conversations she had during community health screening programmes in her first two years of medical school.
Cancer patients and survivors described the emotional burden of the disease, including times between appointments when they had no one to talk to or did not want to burden their families.
Chan said the team had built safeguards into the AI to prevent it from giving medical advice and direct clinical questions to healthcare teams instead.
The team is also mindful of the risk that vulnerable patients could become too dependent on an AI chatbot.
“I don’t see it as replacing human connection. It’s something that can provide support in between,” she said.
The system is intended primarily for people experiencing relatively mild emotional difficulties. Those with moderate or severe mental health needs would still require professional help, and users would be encouraged to maintain real-life connections.
Another safeguard is designed to detect language suggesting self-harm or suicidal thoughts. These cases would be reviewed by a person and, where necessary, referred to social workers or other professionals.
CancerCompanion remains in development and is not yet available as a general patient service. A clinical study to assess the companion’s effects on patients’ mental health and quality of life received ethics approval in August. The system draws on principles of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).

The team has also filed a US provisional patent application for its AI-powered conversational system.
Chan said testing would proceed gradually. Researchers initially plan to observe participants using the system and gather immediate feedback.
In a later phase, patients would use it for four weeks before researchers assessed measures including depression and anxiety scores.
Patient input has guided the project from the outset. The team conducted in-depth interviews with cancer survivors before development began. Survivors, NGO staff and CUHK professors in psychiatry and oncology have since reviewed versions of the system.
Chan said the guiding principle was to develop the technology with patients rather than assume what they needed.
CancerCompanion won the undergraduate group category at the Professor Charles K. Kao Student Creativity Awards in 2025 and was first runner-up in CUHK’s Vice-Chancellor’s Cup of Student Entrepreneurship that year.
Chan’s other work includes a deep-learning project to assess joint conditions at CUHK Rheumatology, which won the Vice-Chancellor’s Cup in 2026. She has also worked on software engineering and embedded programming with the CUHK Robotics Team.
She credited her CancerCompanion teammates and advisers, including CUHK professors in psychiatry and oncology, patient advocates and NGO staff. She also acknowledged the rheumatology researchers advising her master’s research.
Chan plans to return to medical school next year for hospital placements. In the longer term, she hopes to pursue academic medicine, combining research with clinical work.
The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise the city’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

data.title: Growing number of ex-officials enter Hong Kong Election Committee race
data.description:
A growing number of former senior government officials have joined the race for seats on Hong Kong’s Election Committee, a trend observers say will enhance the prestige and legitimacy of the body tasked with choosing the city’s next leader.
As the two-week nomination period draws to a close next Tuesday, the Registration and Electoral Office had received 1,115 nominations for 982 elected seats on the Election Committee as of Friday.
The poll will be held on November 22 and the elected members will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies, to select Hong Kong’s next chief executive in March next year.

A notable feature of this year’s nominations is the number of former senior officials returning to politics.
Former justice minister Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung is standing in the legal subsector, while former health minister Sophia Chan Siu-chee and former undersecretary for health Libby Lee Ha-yun, now the Hospital Authority’s chief executive, are running in the medical and health services subsector.
Former innovation and technology secretary Alfred Sit Wing-hang, former development secretary Eric Ma Siu-cheung, and Wai Chi-sing, former managing director of the Urban Renewal Authority and former permanent secretary for development, are contesting seats in the engineering subsector.
Former financial services and treasury secretary Ceajer Chan Ka-keung, now chairman of WeLab Bank, is seeking re-election in the finance subsector.
Simon Li Tin-chui, former head of the Civil Aviation Department and now president of the Hong Kong International Aviation Academy, is running in the transport subsector, while Annie Tam Kam-lan, former permanent secretary for labour and welfare, is standing in the social welfare subsector.
Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-Hing said the participation of more former officials would improve the committee’s diversity and legitimacy.
“In the past, not many former officials took part in the election committee. Now, not only people from that particular sector are taking part, but also former officials … Their ministerial and government portfolios are broad, which will expand the breadth of election committee members,” he said.
“This also enhances the competitiveness of the poll, which is beneficial to its legitimacy.”
Lo added that former officials had an advantage because they enjoyed Beijing’s trust, which helped ensure political reliability while making the body more pluralistic.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said including more former ministers with extensive political experience would enhance the prestige of the committee.
He added that the trend reflected a broadening of officials’ career paths and would help attract new talent into public service.
Although the ex-officials still have to compete in the election, Lau believed their networks, reputations and political experience accumulated during their tenure would give them an edge in their campaigns.
As in previous polls, major developers have also entered the race, including billionaire Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai, Henderson Land Development chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing and Sino Land chairman Daryl Ng Win-kong, who are seeking re-election.
Other prominent candidates standing include Jardine Matheson executive chairman Benjamin Keswick, Hysan Development executive chairman Irene Lee Yun-lien, Sun Hung Kai Properties executive director Christopher Kwok Kai-wang and CK Asset executive director Justin Chiu Kwok-hung.
Hopefuls also include New World Development executive director Sonia Cheng Chi-man and Shangri-La Group chairman and CEO Kuok Hui Kwong.
Several leading bankers have also submitted nominations. They include HSBC’s vice-chairman for Hong Kong, Diana Cesar; HSBC co-CEO for Asia and the Middle East David Liao Yi-chien; Citi Hong Kong CEO and head of banking Aveline San Pau-len; Standard Chartered Bank’s CEO for Hong Kong, Greater China and North Asia, Mary Huen Wai-yi; and Bank of East Asia co-chief executive Adrian David Li Man-kiu.
Other high-profile candidates include table tennis player and Olympic medallist Doo Hoi-kem and blind singer Michelle Siu Hoi-yan.
The 1,500 members of the election committee will be responsible for nominating and selecting the city leader next March and electing 40 of the Legislative Council’s 90 members in 2029.
The committee comprises five sectors representing 40 subsectors, ranging from commercial, financial and professional groups to labour unions, district representatives and Hong Kong representatives on national bodies.
The full list of nominations can be seen here.

data.title: LVMH touts ‘special bond’ with China amid ‘subdued’ sales backdrop
data.description:
French luxury giant LVMH Group kicked off a global open-house event showcasing its craftsmanship in Shanghai on Thursday, as the event’s founder Antoine Arnault hailed a “special bond” with Chinese customers at a launch event in Paris.
It came as the group faced pressure from sluggish demand in China and a backlash over a lawsuit against a local tea company.
At the launch event at the Samaritaine department store in central Paris for this year’s Les Journées Particulières, first initiated by Arnault in 2011, he mentioned the Shanghai event, which was the first among 71 venues across 13 countries to open to the public for the three-day event.
“For the first time since the event was created, several LVMH houses have come together in a single venue to share our savoir faire and its dialogue with Chinese culture,” said Arnault, who holds multiple roles within LVMH and is the son of its chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault. “Because we share a special bond with China and our Chinese customers.”
The exhibition in Shanghai will gather 15 brands from the group, including Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine, Tiffany and Bulgari. Visitors will get a behind-the-scenes look at how some of the group’s iconic products are made, such as Louis Vuitton’s Speedy P9 bag.
LVMH held an opening ceremony in Zhangyuan, a historic neighbourhood near Nanjing Xilu, on Thursday, featuring a Chinese calligraphy ceremony.
Four venues in China will participate in this year’s event: two in Shanghai and one each in Hong Kong and Ningxia.

The event came as the group announced disappointing numbers from China earlier this week in its third-quarter results: sales declined 5 per cent in Asia excluding Japan, caused mainly by a sharp macro-led deterioration in Chinese consumer sentiment, according to the group.
Louis Vuitton’s lawsuit against local brand Molly Tea further complicated the situation for the French luxury giant in the world’s second biggest luxury market.
The local tea chain was ordered by a Chinese court to pay 10.3 million yuan (US$1.5 million) in restitution in July over its use of a logo similar to the French brand’s four-petaled flower. The initial ruling, despite the appeal, sparked heated online debate and drew public sympathy for the Chinese company.
“[It’s] very difficult to size a precise impact, but it’s probably fair to say that it had a negative impact, at least at the beginning of the quarter,” said Cecile Cabanis, LVMH’s chief financial officer, during an earnings call on Monday.
“The news flow has not been particularly good in China in the summer, so this has really weighed on the feel-good factor and created a short-term subdued Chinese backdrop. We hope it will subside. We need to do more, but we have not stopped investing in China.”
Like in previous years, LVMH will participate in this year’s China International Import Expo, set for Shanghai early next month.

data.title: Hong Kong police arrest 2 men over HK$1.7 million Kowloon break-in spree
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested two men over their alleged involvement in at least six break-ins across Kowloon over the past three months, with total losses amounting to HK$1.7 million (US$216,629).
The pair – a 54-year-old mainland Chinese man and a 34-year-old Hong Kong resident – were arrested separately on Thursday in Sham Shui Po and Tsim Sha Tsui, respectively.
Police identified and located them following a break-in targeting four flats in a private residential building on Farm Road in Kowloon City, where more than HK$100,000 in cash and watches, as well as some credit cards, were stolen.
At a press briefing on Friday, Tsang Ka-chun, a senior inspector with the Kowloon City district crime squad, said police attached great importance to the case and were able to identify and locate the two suspects after reviewing surveillance camera footage.
Initial investigations showed that the pair generally targeted private residential homes with unlocked windows or doors, while the flats were unoccupied at night.
“The mainland man would break into the flats and steal valuables. He would subsequently hand over the stolen credit cards to the Hong Kong man, who used them to make online purchases totalling around HK$30,000,” Tsang said.
“After subsequent investigations, detectives also believe the duo are connected with at least five burglary cases that took place in Kowloon City and Cheung Sha Wan between July and October,” he added.
In those cases, about HK$1.6 million in cash, handbags and jewellery were stolen.
The mainlander was arrested for attempted burglary and illegal immigration, while the local man was arrested for handling stolen goods and obtaining property by deception.
During Thursday’s operation, officers seized cash, credit cards and valuables, as well as clothes and shoes believed to belong to the suspects.
The two men remained in police custody for questioning on Friday evening.
Tsang urged flat owners to remain vigilant and take simple precautions, such as locking windows and doors before leaving home, and to install surveillance cameras.
Under the Theft Ordinance, the maximum penalty upon conviction for burglary or handling stolen goods is 14 years’ imprisonment, while obtaining property by deception carries a maximum sentence of 10 years.
Hong Kong logged 344 burglary cases in the first half of 2026, down 22.7 per cent from 445 in the same period last year, according to police statistics.
Burglaries fell to a record low of 818 cases, a 33.1 per cent year-on-year drop, in 2025.

data.title: AI-powered drones to help detect hill fires during Chung Yeung Festival
data.description:
Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department will launch three new AI-assisted drone technologies to strengthen fire detection and its response to heightened risks during tomb-sweeping activities ahead of the Chung Yeung Festival on Sunday.
Wong Tak-fai, acting divisional officer for information and communications technology, said on Friday that the technology would improve the speed and accuracy of fire detection to help the department operate more efficiently.
“Artificial intelligence [AI] not only speeds up the processing of drone images but, more importantly, helps our staff continuously analyse large amounts of images from different drones across various locations to identify situations needing priority attention,” Wong said.
With the Chung Yeung Festival approaching, the department will strengthen manpower to monitor high-risk locations for fires and step up district patrols and public education efforts with the Civil Aid Service and other district organisations.
The department will also deploy 159 firefighters on Saturday across 12 locations in New Territories North, 10 spots in Kowloon and another six locations in New Territories South. On Sunday, an additional 166 firefighters will be deployed.
Hong Kong recorded 693 hill fires in 2025.
The department will also mobilise a newly bought remotely operated aerial surveillance system consisting of an off-road vehicle from mainland Chinese manufacturer Geely retrofitted with two drone docking systems and a generator.
The HK$1.2 million system will allow officers to survey hard-to-reach fire hazard areas. Its drones can conduct automated patrols within a 3km radius and be controlled remotely.

A real-time artificial intelligence video analysis platform will also be used to speed up the analysis of drone footage and images to generate timely alerts for fire hazards or drownings.
The system uses AI to accurately identify signs of smoke and people who may be drowning, reducing the need for staff to review drone surveillance footage.
“The new platform will be able to receive the footage in real time during a drone flight and then simultaneously run an artificial intelligence analysis,” Wong said.
Currently, footage analysis takes place after a flight ends, with officers manually transferring the files from an SD card in the drone to a computer.
The department will also have two high-payload drones equipped with water-bomb systems ready for deployment against remote hill fires. Each drone costs HK$500,000, including batteries.
These drones can carry weights up to 150kg and are equipped with an 80-litre water tank, allowing them to release water bombs where needed.
Wong said that in departmental tests, while it took firefighters one hour to carry rescue equipment 5km uphill, the large drone could do it in 10 minutes.
“The Fire Services Department is exploring the use of large drones in frontline operations, hoping to move from surveillance and observation to delivering firefighting equipment,” Wong said.
However, the acting divisional officer said artificial intelligence would in no way replace firefighters, as he stressed that all operational decisions would still be made by humans.

data.title: ASML eyes hybrid bonding, report finds, as Chinese firms adopt chip technique
data.description:
Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML is expanding into next-generation hybrid bonding, a technique that creates dense electrical connections by directly joining chips or silicon wafers, according to a new report. Major Chinese companies are also adopting the technology to improve chip performance.
ASML submitted 27 patent families related to hybrid bonding tools between December 2022 and November 2024, according to a report published by semiconductor and AI supply chain research firm SemiAnalysis on Thursday. The number could be higher because of publication delays affecting recent filings, it said.
The filings suggest ASML is moving beyond lithography, a market it dominates, into back-end processes as demand for high-performance chips surges amid the global artificial intelligence boom.
The company had also begun developing the architecture for a hybrid bonder with Dutch technology firms Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG, according to SemiAnalysis, citing industry media reports.
“We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for hybrid bonding,” SemiAnalysis said. “These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography.”
The company has not officially announced the extent of its progress on advanced packaging. But CEO Christophe Fouquet said during an April earnings call that the company was “continuing to look for opportunities to support our customers” in hybrid bonding.
ASML told the South China Morning Post by email on Friday that it would “continue to look in which directions [the] 3D integration industry will evolve and to see how this relates to ASML’s roadmap, and where ASML’s expertise can be of added value”.
Hybrid bonding allows ultra-high-density electrical connections and is widely viewed as one of the next major trends in chipmaking. Recent breakthroughs by China’s Huawei Technologies and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) involved using the technique to improve performance as United States-led export restrictions limit access to some advanced semiconductor equipment.


Under those restrictions, Huawei and CXMT cannot import ASML’s most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines.
Hybrid bonding can reduce the thermal resistance in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks by about 30 per cent, according to a September report by Guotai Haitong Securities, which cited Samsung data. Lower thermal resistance can help heat escape more easily, potentially reducing cooling requirements and the need for related investments.
Huawei disclosed new details this week about its flagship Kirin 9050 series, the first mass-produced chip to use its proprietary LogicFolding architecture developed under a framework it calls the Tau Scaling Law. The company said the design integrated more than 50 million hybrid bonds and increased overall transistor density by 53.5 per cent.
CXMT, meanwhile, announced last week that its latest “4F square” dynamic random-access memory architecture used hybrid bonding, which could allow it to increase wafer bit density without relying on advanced EUV lithography.
Despite the potential benefits of the technique, China remained heavily dependent on imported hybrid bonding equipment, particularly advanced machines, according to a separate report by Huaan Securities.
The report noted that domestic equipment manufacturers were stepping up research and development to narrow the gap, with Piotech and Xinhui Lianxin among the leading players.
Piotech’s hybrid bonding equipment generated 136 million yuan (US$20.3 million) in revenue in 2025, up 41.9 per cent from a year earlier, according to its annual report.
Nomura analysts said in a report last week that Huawei’s LogicFolding architecture could drive demand for bonding equipment, as well as Piotech’s mainstay thin-film deposition tools.

data.title: 3 arrested over missing fire-safety parts in 48 Hong Kong lifts, source says
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested a director and two registered lift engineers on suspicion of deception in connection with faulty replacement works on 48 lifts at two housing estates, the South China Morning Post has learned.
The latest suspected faults come just months after a fiasco involving lifts at a new hospital block, and experts said on Friday a thorough review of the regulatory process could be needed
A source said the three suspects were from Taizoom Elevator, which replaced nine lifts at Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong and 39 lifts at Pok Hong Estate in Sha Tin.
One of the suspects was a 79-year-old director and shareholder of Taizoom. The other two were registered lift engineers who examined the installations and signed safety certificates, aged 63 and 82, respectively.

The arrests came a day after the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department said its inspection, triggered by a complaint, found that Taizoom had installed fire-resistant doors without the required door frame components at the two estates.
The department said the contractor had submitted a fire-resisting rating certificate and claimed it had completed the works.
Suspecting fraud and false statements, the department reported the case to police.
The insider said officers raided the company’s office in Chai Wan, and the investigation had found that the outstanding components were “critical smoke control devices”.
“The registered contractor and the registered engineer responsible for inspecting the lifts allegedly concealed the construction defects intentionally and falsely reported to the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department and the owners’ corporation that the works were completed in accordance with the contract,” the source said.
The case has been referred to the regional crime unit of New Territories South.
According to the department’s quarterly performance rating for lift contractors, Taizoom scored three out of five in service quality and had the same score in safety performance as other companies.
The arrests came two months after 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new 34-storey clinical block were deemed unfit for use.
Law Wing-chai, a registered lift engineer involved in the hospital project, was sentenced to 160 hours of community service last month after being convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates.

Professor Ho Wing-ip, an adjunct professor at Polytechnic University’s department of electrical and electronic engineering, said both incidents might have been the result of lapses in supervision and a thorough review could be needed.
“After the two incidents, the public’s trust in registered lift engineers seems to have been shaken a bit ... We still do not know if they are just the tip of an iceberg or extremely rare cases. The department has to look thoroughly into the sector and report to the public,” he said.
“If they are the tip of an iceberg, then it requires a review of the existing system and mechanism.”
A lift can only go into service after the director of electrical and mechanical services issues or renews the required permit.
Only registered lift contractors can undertake works, which should be examined by a registered lift engineer.
Ho said the door frame components were intended to prevent flames and smoke from seeping through gaps if a fire broke out.
Typically, door frame components were only visible from the top of the lift car, he explained, adding that the department might have to request registered lift engineers to inspect them and include photos as records in the examination report.
Ho noted that lifts underwent monthly maintenance and annual inspections, but given the number in the city, checking every concealed part each time was unrealistic.
According to official information from February, Hong Kong had 73,393 lifts.
Louis Szeto Ka-sing, past chairman of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers’ mechanical, marine, naval architecture and chemical division, said authorities should first check whether similar problems existed in other lifts.
He pointed out that the problem might not only involve the contractor, registered lift professionals and the department, but also the supplier of the lift components, logistics parties, workers and work supervisors.
Szeto said it was possible the stakeholders had failed to communicate properly and could not identify the risks in advance.
“We have to look into the incident,” he said. “Only training and communication can help resolve potential risks.”
The department said on Thursday that it had started a comprehensive review of the installation of new equipment and lift modernisation, inspection and maintenance works, site supervision system and systems under the Lifts and Escalators Ordinance.

data.title: China’s AI infrastructure boom fuels earnings surge for local chip firms
data.description:
Chinese chip and tech firms have flagged as much as six-fold growth in unaudited third-quarter profits, as huge demand for home-grown processors and artificial intelligence infrastructure filters through links in the supply chain amid the country’s push for self-reliance.
Shanghai-listed Yuanjie Semiconductor Technology expected its quarterly net profit to land between 403 million yuan and 453 million yuan, up 579 per cent to 660 per cent from a year earlier.
The maker of laser chips for optical communications said data-centre demand was driving shipments and helping maintain high margins.
Some public firms offered a glimpse of their financial performance in the first nine months of the year, ahead of final third-quarter results announcements.
Graphics processing unit (GPU) designer MetaX, listed in Shanghai but also pursuing a Hong Kong listing, turned a profit in the period thanks to increasing orders. It estimated a net profit of between 587 million yuan (US$88 million) and 717 million yuan, reversing a year-earlier loss, even excluding non-recurring gains.

Hygon Information, whose processors serve both general computing and AI workloads, projected revenue growth of 50 per cent to 64 per cent in the first nine months. It cited rising demand for high-end chips as customers increasingly choose domestic alternatives over foreign suppliers.
Storage giant Shenzhen Longsys Electronics said its net profit during the period could reach 14 billion to 14.9 billion yuan, roughly 20 times the figure for the previous year. It noted that price increases for DRAM and NAND flash storage had slowed in the third quarter, giving profits a smaller boost.
Memory prices could remain firm through 2027, according to a Morgan Stanley report on Sunday, which also warned that supply catching up or customers slowing their purchases could cool the boom even without weaker AI demand.
Optical module supplier Accelink Technologies forecast a nine-month net profit growth of 65 per cent to 82 per cent, citing both global AI capital spending and Chinese cloud providers’ continued investment in data centres as profit drivers.
Silicon wafer supplier Xian Eswin Material Technology said its production lines ran at full capacity in the first nine months, with sales volumes up about 43 per cent to 8.3 million wafers. Although its net profit of about 151 million yuan during the period was boosted by gains from investments in initial public offerings by its customers, it still expected a loss after excluding non-recurring items.
China’s AI buildout and efforts to replace imported processors are bringing more business to local chip designers. Research firm TrendForce projected in August that Chinese-designed chips would account for almost 90 per cent of the country’s high-end AI processor market this year.
The growth in chip production is also lifting materials suppliers. Hubei Feilihua Quartz Glass forecast nine-month net profit growth of 35 per cent to 56 per cent, citing stronger semiconductor demand and opportunities to replace imported products.
The research firm Bernstein said in a Tuesday report that quartz components used in chipmaking equipment were already well localised in China, with further growth increasingly tied to orders for domestic chipmaking equipment.

data.title: Inspections ordered at 8 more houses in One Stanley after rebar scandal
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities have ordered the developer of the One Stanley luxury estate to inspect eight more houses – including one acquired by a Mongolian mining tycoon’s family – and the common area of a flat, in the wake of a scandal involving alleged substandard works at a building in the residential development.
The details of the inspection were announced in a sales brochure updated on Friday by K&K Property, the developer of the neighbourhood in southern Hong Kong, after a detached house, No 35, was alleged to be defective due to insufficient steel bars used in parts of the building.
The Buildings Department announced in early October that it would conduct random checks on buildings in the estate, after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said he had tasked the Development Bureau to closely monitor the investigation into the case.
According to the brochure, the department had spotted irregularities in the house, including the absence of wire mesh on the concrete cover of a ground-floor beam, as required by the approved plan, and deviations in the steel reinforcement of some slabs.
The department told the developer to inspect houses No 5, 8, 16, 17, 19, 32, 33 and 36, as well as the common area of a flat, Block 9.
According to a source familiar with the matter, buyers had signed provisional purchase agreements on three of the houses – No 5, 16 and 17 – but none had requested to terminate the contracts so far.
The South China Morning Post earlier reported that Tisara Holdings, whose director is Tselmuun Nyamtaishir, signed a provisional agreement in January to purchase the No 5 house.
Nyamtaishir is the president and CEO of Mongolyn Alt (MAK), a mineral conglomerate founded in 1993 by her father in Mongolia and is the largest coal exporter in the country.
She earlier told the SCMP that the block was intended to be used as the retirement residence of the group’s founders.
Land Registry records show house No 16 was sold to Supreme Harmony Limited at HK$116.8 million (US$14.9 million). The company, whose owner is a mainland Chinese national, signed the sale and purchase agreement in June this year.
House No 17 was sold for HK$118 million to an individual, who signed the document in August.
The Buildings Department declined on Friday to comment on further investigation details.
Speaking to the press on Thursday, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho also declined to provide more details about the case, saying the investigation into No 35 by the Buildings Department was still ongoing.

Asked why the department deemed it appropriate to issue an occupation permit for the house, Linn said some problems might remain hidden to authorities.
“Sometimes, when an occupation permit is issued, there may be hidden areas that were not visible at the time,” she said.
“We will definitely make the investigation results public, act in accordance with the law, and punish offenders according to law.”
The issue first came to light after online property news outlet WuChatProp said on October 2 that an on-site inspection of the house found insufficient steel bars were used in some parts of the building, and the amount in certain areas fell short of the approved structural plan by as much as 75 per cent.
The owner, who submitted a complaint to the department in January, had lamented the government’s inaction, according to the report.
The property is a four-bedroom, 3,000-square-foot (278 square metre) detached house, which the owner reportedly bought in 2024. The price stood at HK$115.8 million, according to a transaction list obtained by the SCMP.
The problem was discovered as Hong Kong was hit with a string of construction scandals, including issues with concrete samples from three public housing blocks under construction in Tung Chung, prompting further review and testing in September.
Earlier in August, 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block were deemed unfit for use. The widespread installation defects delayed the full commissioning of the Pok Fu Lam hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year.
City leader Lee declined to comment on individual cases but said he was concerned as to whether the professionals involved in the projects had discharged their duties properly, adding that such matters concerned professional standards and the quality and safety of the city’s construction works.
In response to the scandal at One Stanley, K Wise, a subsidiary of K&K Property, said it would offer a six-year structural warranty to One Stanley homeowners and would also arrange free independent inspections.
It also said the owner and the developer had agreed to jointly hire an independent surveyor to determine the circumstances, while no other consensus was reached.
